root.name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit: Rasa-Studier Gambit
root.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. e4 dxe4 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. Be3

parent.name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit
parent.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. e4 dxe4 3. Nc3 Nf6
parent.overview: White offers a pawn with 1.d4 d5 2.e4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3, aiming for rapid development, the open f-file and a kingside attack with Bc4, Nge2 or Bf4, castling, g4/h4 and Qe1-h4 ideas against h7. Black accepts with 4...exf3 5.Nxf3 and can choose among the Euwe (5...e6), Ziegler (5...c6), Teichmann (5...Bg4) and Bogoljubov (5...g6) defences, or decline with the Lemberger Countergambit 3...e5. With accurate defence Black consolidates the pawn, trades pieces and heads for a better endgame; engines and master opinion call White's compensation insufficient, which is why it is almost never seen at top level. Below master level it scores very well because the attack is easy to play and hard to defend against. The game is typically open and tactical.

root.name: Sicilian Defense: Quinteros Variation
root.moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 Qc7

parent.name: Sicilian Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 1.e4 with ...c5 to trade a flank pawn for White's d-pawn, which leaves Black a central pawn majority and a half-open c-file in return for White's lead in development and space. This asymmetry is the point: Black plays for a win rather than equality. The usual pattern is White attacking on the kingside while Black counterattacks on the queenside along the c-file (...b5, ...Rc8), often with opposite-side castling in the sharpest lines. The root is a crossroads: after 2.Nf3 (about 80% of master games, s1) it branches into Najdorf, Dragon, Scheveningen, Classical, Sveshnikov, Taimanov and Kan, which range from forcing and theory-heavy (Najdorf, Dragon, Sveshnikov) to flexible and solid (Kan, Classical, Taimanov). White's anti-Sicilians (Alapin, Closed, Grand Prix, 2.d3) avoid the Open Sicilian and are quieter. The root as a whole is the most played and most analysed opening at club and master level (s1).

parent.name: Polish Opening
parent.overview: White plays 1.b4 to grab queenside space and fianchetto the bishop to b2, putting long-diagonal pressure on e5, f6 and g7. It is an irregular flank opening: Black chooses the set-up with 1...e5 (2.Bb2 Bxb4 3.Bxe5, the Exchange Variation, which equalises), 1...d5 (the German Defence 2...Qd6 etc.), or 1...Nf6 and 1...e6 reaching Indian-like or Queen's Gambit-like set-ups. The opening is sound and not refuted but gives Black no real problems, so it is rarely seen at elite level and chosen as a surprise weapon (Carlsen used it against Nakamura and So in 2021). Theory is small and the play is flank-oriented, with unbalanced pawn structures but typically no early forced tactics. Alekhine's complaint was that it reveals White's intentions before knowing Black's.

parent.name: Nimzo-Larsen Attack: Classical Variation
parent.overview: White fianchettoes the queen's bishop on b2 to influence the centre from the flank and the long diagonal, while Black takes the classical centre with 1...d5. Against ...d5 White usually develops first (Bb2, Nf3, e3), stays flexible, and only then decides between c4, d3 or d4, keeping the b2 bishop relevant to every central decision. Typical lines are 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.e3 e6 (and 4.Bb5+ or c4 set-ups) or 2...c5. The line is a recognised system: themes (dark-square control, e5, Bb5, Ne5, f4, sometimes queenside castling with g4-h4) matter more than heavy theory. Sources agree Black equalises comfortably with natural development, but White gets practical chances, especially in fast time controls; it is used by strong players (Larsen, Carlsen, Nakamura) mainly as a surprise or to avoid main repertoire lines.

root.name: Center Game: Ross Gambit
root.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. d4 exd4 3. Bd3

parent.name: Center Game Accepted
parent.overview: The root is the crossroads after 2.d4 exd4, with Black a pawn up and White to move. White's main choice is 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qe3 (Paulsen Attack): the pawn is regained, Black gains a tempo on the queen, and White castles queenside after Nc3 and Bd2, using the queen on e3 and the d-file to aim at g7 and the kingside. Black has calm, sound ways to equalise (4...Nf6, 4...Be7 preparing ...d5, 4...g6, 4...Bb4+) and can counterattack White's king on the queenside. The alternative 3.c3 is the Danish Gambit, where White gives one or two pawns for open lines and development. 3.Nf3 or 3.Bc4 lead to Scotch, Scotch Gambit, Petroff-type or Urusov positions. Overall it is old and rarely played at the top level, though with a modern revival (Shabalov, then Nepomniachtchi and Erigaisi, Shirov, Adams) as a practical, objectively equal surprise.

root.name: Ruy Lopez: Lucena Variation
root.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5 Be7

parent.name: Ruy Lopez
parent.overview: The Ruy Lopez is the most extensively developed Open Game. 3.Bb5 attacks the knight that defends e5, building indirect pressure on the e5 pawn without the Italian's vulnerability to ...d5. This root (3.Bb5) is a crossroads: after the most common 3...a6 (about two-thirds of games) the Closed Spanish (4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 d6 8.c3 O-O 9.h3) leads to a slow, locked-centre manoeuvring game; the Berlin (3...Nf6 4.O-O Nxe4) gives a solid, drawish endgame-flavoured structure; the Marshall Attack is a sharp Black pawn sacrifice. White's central plan is c3 and d4 plus the Nbd2-f1-g3 knight route, while Black counterattacks on the queenside (...b5, ...Na5, ...c5) or breaks with ...d5. Theory is the deepest of any 1.e4 opening.
